hints: Keep the lower half in a max heap and upper half in a min heap.
Balance sizes after each add.
problems.approach: Implement the two-heap median with balanced max/min heaps.
problems.solution: Push each value into the correct half, rebalance so sizes differ by at most one, and read the median from the roots.

problems.name: Sliding Window Median
problems.description: Return the median of every window of size k as it slides over an array.
hints: Extend two heaps with lazy deletion for removals.
Track stale entries and clean heap tops.
problems.approach: Keep two heaps for the current window; on each slide add the new value and lazily remove the old one, then rebalance and read the median.
problems.solution: Maintain the lower/upper heaps for the window. Add new elements normally; for evictions, mark a removal count and pop stale heap tops before reading the median.

problems.name: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problems.description: Return the median of two sorted arrays in O(log(min(m, n))) time.
hints: Binary search the partition point in the smaller array.
The two halves must satisfy the cross-order conditions.
problems.approach: Binary search the cut in the smaller array so that left partitions of both arrays combine into the left half; check max-left <= min-right.
problems.solution: Partition the smaller array with binary search and derive the cut in the larger one. Adjust the cut until every left element is <= every right element, then read the median from the boundary elements.

name: Heap / Priority Queue
overview: This category covers the heap data structure and the priority queue abstraction built on it: inserting and extracting the best element in O(log n), building heaps in O(n), and the problem family they power (top-k, median, scheduling, merging).
why: Heap and priority queue patterns recur across many interview topics. Recognizing when a problem needs 'repeatedly take the min/max of a changing set' is a high-value skill that generalizes beyond any single problem.
when: Reach for a heap/PQ when the solution repeatedly needs the smallest or largest element of a dynamically changing collection, or when items must be processed in priority order.

complexity.time: O(log n) per insert/extract, O(1) peek

concepts.name: Heap property
concepts.description: A parent is always <= (min heap) or >= (max heap) its children.

concepts.name: Priority queue ADT
concepts.description: The interface contract: insert, peek, and extract the best element.

concepts.name: Two-heap pattern
concepts.description: Pairing a max and min heap to maintain a running order statistic like the median.

concepts.name: K-way merge
concepts.description: Using a heap to merge several sorted sequences by always consuming the smallest head.

concepts.name: Greedy with heap
concepts.description: Always act on the current best candidate, re-inserting new candidates after acting.

concepts.name: Lazy deletion
concepts.description: Marking stale entries and cleaning them when they reach the top, used in sliding windows.

patterns.name: Two-heap median
patterns.description: Balanced max/min heaps answer median queries in O(1).
patterns.code:
import heapq
lo, hi = [], []
for x in stream:
    heapq.heappush(lo, -x)
    heapq.heappush(hi, -heapq.heappop(lo))
    if len(lo) < len(hi):
        heapq.heappush(lo, -heapq.heappop(hi))

patterns.name: K-way merge
patterns.description: Merge k sorted lists by always popping the minimum head.
patterns.code:
import heapq
h = [(lst[0], i, 0) for i, lst in enumerate(lists) if lst]
heapq.heapify(h)
out = []
while h:
    v, i, j = heapq.heappop(h)
    out.append(v)
    if j + 1 < len(lists[i]):
        heapq.heappush(h, (lists[i][j + 1], i, j + 1))

patterns.name: Top-k via heap
patterns.description: Keep the k best with a k-sized heap and evict the worst.

examples.title: When to reach for a heap
examples.problem: Pick a heap-based solution over a sort or linear scan.
examples.input: repeated 'best of' queries on a changing collection
examples.output: use a heap (O(log n) per update)
examples.explanation: If you must repeatedly grab the min/max while data changes, a sort recomputes O(n log n) each time; a heap costs O(log n) per operation.
steps: If the collection changes between queries, use a heap
If the collection is static, a single sort then O(1) reads is better
Choose min or max heap by which end is queried

mistakes.mistake: Sorting repeatedly on changing data instead of using a heap.
mistakes.fix: Use a heap for dynamic best-element access; reserve sorting for static data.

mistakes.mistake: Neglecting the comparator when priorities are tuples or objects.
mistakes.fix: Store (priority, counter, payload) so ordering is total and deterministic.

mistakes.mistake: Using a heap when the array is static and a sort plus prefix logic suffices.
mistakes.fix: For a one-shot query, sorting is O(n log n) once and simpler than heap bookkeeping.

problems.name: Design Twitter
problems.description: Design a simplified Twitter with postTweet, getNewsFeed, follow, and unfollow.
problems.constraints: users and tweets up to 10^4, feed size 10
hints: Keep each user's tweets with a global timestamp.
Merge the feeds of followed users with a max heap.
problems.approach: Store tweets per user with a global counter; for the feed, push each followed user's recent tweets into a max heap and pop the top 10.
problems.time: O(f log f) per feed query
problems.solution: Maintain per-user tweet lists and a follow map. To build a feed, push the latest tweets of the user and all followed users into a max heap ordered by timestamp and pop ten.

problems.name: Longest Happy String
problems.description: Build the longest string from a, b, c letters avoiding three consecutive identical letters.
hints: Always append the most abundant letter allowed.
A max heap of (count, letter) works.
problems.approach: Push (count, letter) into a max heap; each step take the most abundant letter not equal to the last two, and allow the previously blocked letter back.
problems.solution: Repeatedly pick the letter with the largest remaining count that is not the same as the last two placed; if it would repeat, pick the next best, then decrement and push back.

problems.name: Course Schedule III
problems.description: Return the maximum number of courses you can take given duration and last-day deadlines.
hints: Sort by deadline.
A max heap of durations lets you drop the longest course when time exceeds a deadline.
problems.approach: Sort by deadline; take courses greedily, and when total time exceeds the current deadline, remove the longest-duration course taken so far.
problems.solution: Sort by deadline ascending. Add each course's duration to a running total and a max heap; if the total exceeds the deadline, pop the longest duration, restoring feasibility. Heap size is the answer.
